# Simultaneous Matrix Multiplication by Tensor Contraction Aggregation

**Abstract**

We present an interpretation of the fast matrix multiplication algorithms of Coppersmith and Winograd as aggregations of tensor contractions. This point of view provides a direct connection to older constructions by Pan and to more recent work on bilinear algorithms for symmetric tensor contraction. Further, we provide a simple explicit approach for exact aggregation of tensor contractions, each one yielding an independent matrix-matrix product. These constructions and border rank adaptations thereof do not come close to improving the best known bounds on \(\omega\) (the matrix multiplication exponent), but provide explicit moderate-size fast matrix multiplication algorithms that achieve a better exponent than Strassen’s algorithm and have potential practical value. These finite constructions improve the multiplication-count bounds of the reference algorithms compared here for selected numbers and dimensions of independent square matrix products. In particular, using \(\langle m,m,m\rangle\) to denote the matrix multiplication tensor for matrices of dimension _m_, we obtain constructions that give bounds such as the border rank bound

\(\underline{R}\big(\langle n^2,n^2,n^2\rangle^{\oplus 9}\big)\le(n+1)^6+6(n+1)^5,\)

and the exact rank bound

\(R\big(\langle n^3,n^3,n^3\rangle^{\oplus 14}\big)\le(n+1)^9.\)

We quantify the accuracy of such constructions in finite precision, and provide border-rank constructions that reduce cost with limiting retained fractions of accuracy at least 1/2, 1/3, or 1/4 relative to the classical matrix-multiplication approach under the stated error model.

### 1 Introduction

Independent matrix-matrix products are a key subject in the theoretical study of the matrix multiplication exponent, \(\omega\). Schönhage’s asymptotic sum theorem [30] gives upper bounds on \(\omega\) based on constructions for independent matrix-matrix products, and the extensively studied method of Coppersmith and Winograd [15] provides efficient border-rank constructions for such sets of products. Exact-rank bounds for balanced restrictions of these tensor powers, and hence for balanced compatible families of independent products, were established by Flavi, Jelisiejew, and Michałek [20]. Their work builds on the group-tensor formulation of Alman and Vassilevska Williams [3]. At the same time, independent matrix-matrix products are in themselves a common computational kernel, frequently arising in dense and sparse linear algebra, for instance when multiplying block-sparse matrices [11]. In recent years, standard software interfaces and libraries have been developed for independent matrix-matrix multiplications [1]. In this paper, we develop a new, more practical point of view on the Coppersmith–Winograd construction by considering aggregation of tensor contractions.

Aggregation of two matrix multiplications is a technique employed by Victor Pan in his matrix multiplication constructions \[25, 27\]. We recall his construction here as a trilinear form identity. For \(A,B,D,U,V,W\in\mathbb{C}^{n\times n}\), define<tbc>

\(S=\sum_{i,j,h}(a_{ij}+u_{jh})(b_{jh}+v_{hi})(d_{hi}+w_{ij}),\) (1)

\(p_{ih}=\sum_j(a_{ij}+u_{jh}),q_{ij}=\sum_h(b_{jh}+v_{hi}),r_{jh}=\sum_i(d_{hi}+w_{ij}).\) (2)

<tbc>Then

\(\mathrm{tr}(ABD)+\mathrm{tr}(UVW)=S-\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}q_{ij}w_{ij}-\sum_{j,h}u_{jh}b_{jh}r_{jh}-\sum_{h,i}p_{ih}v_{hi}d_{hi}.\) (3)

Hence, two independent products of \(n\times n\) matrices may be computed using _n_<sup>3</sup>+3_n_<sup>2</sup> bilinear multiplications. Leveraging border rank, Pan reduces the count further to _n_<sup>3</sup>+2_n_<sup>2</sup> \[26, Eq. (3.1)\].

In his 1982 work, Pan remarks that his construction computes _AB+BA_ with fewer nonscalar multiplications than his construction for _AB_ \[26, Remark 6.1, p. 33\]. In recent years, a family of algorithms has also been introduced for symmetric tensor contraction \[35\]. For example, for symmetric \(A,B\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\), _C=AB+BA_ may be computed by forming the symmetrized aggregate

\(z_{ijk}=(a_{ij}+a_{ik}+a_{jk})(b_{ij}+b_{ik}+b_{jk}),i<j<k,\) (4)

and applying lower-order corrections, using a total of _n_<sup>3</sup>/6+_O(n_<sup>2</sup>) bilinear multiplications \[35\]. A similar sum over subsets works for higher-order tensor contractions \[35\]. Instead of symmetrization, we consider an analogous aggregation of independent tensor contractions. In Section 5, we show that aggregation of independent tensor contractions is exactly the task performed by the filtered powers of the little and big Coppersmith-Winograd tensors.

We give a direct tensor-contraction formulation of exact decompositions for compatible sets of independent matrix-matrix products. We achieve this using tensor products of a simple centering embedding from C_<sup>n</sup>_ into the zero-sum subspace of C<sup>_n_+1</sup>. We further augment the centering embedding with a weighting, yielding a weighted embedding from C_<sup>n</sup>_ to C<sup>_n_+2</sup> that eliminates both linearly reducible and replicated cross terms. For square matrix products, each contraction is a trilinear form corresponding to a balanced tripartition of 3_N_ indices, and our approach can simultaneously compute any set of such contractions, so long as no recombination of parts from different selected tripartitions is itself a tripartition. This combinatorial condition is the same one addressed by Coppersmith and Winograd using Salem-Spencer sets \[15, 29\].

Besides the exact-rank constructions for independent square matrix products, we also consider aggregation of contractions corresponding to incomplete and unbalanced tripartitions. We show that this space includes the big Coppersmith-Winograd tensor construction \[15\] (Section 5.1). Further, using a standard border-rank degeneration approach \[9\], we loosen the compatibility conditions on tripartitions, enabling aggregation of a larger number of independent matrix-matrix products.

We quantify the parameter conditioning of these graded constructions, estimating the fraction of working- precision digits retained. Our bounds quantify the sensitivity of the bilinear algorithms obtained by the border-rank (graded) constructions to perturbations of their factor maps and bilinear products. These characterizations enable us to target constructions with a specified limiting fraction of retained accuracy, such as half the digits guaranteed by the classical error bound as working precision increases.

With the general aggregation framework established, we then use numerical search to find sets of tripartitions that are compatible for aggregation. The asymptotic exponential growth rate of classical conflict-free tripartition families is characterized by Coppersmith and Winograd \[15\], while numerical search enables us to find constructions of moderate size. Our constructions improve on the prior exact and border-rank multiplication-count bounds compared here for certain moderate numbers _p_ of independent matrix-matrix products and matrix dimensions _q_.

In one of the simplest new constructions, we show that 14 matrix multiplications of matrices of dimension _n_<sup>3</sup> can be aggregated and computed with (_n_+1)<sup>9</sup> bilinear multiplications, instead of the naive 14_n_<sup>9</sup> (Appendix F). We catalogue and compare the new constructions to prior art in Section 8. Figure 4 shows an<tbc>

<tbc>overview of these results, comparing selected prior finite-base constructions with the new variants at finite _p_ and _q_.

The largest exact construction we consider computes _p_=105 independent products of dimension _q=n_<sup>4</sup>, while graded constructions give _p_=125,133,141 with limiting fractions of retained precision at least 1/2,1/3,1/4, respectively (Section 8.2).  1 gives multiplication-count reduction factors of the new construction over LITA, Strassen, and classical multiplication at _q_=11<sup>4</sup>=14641. For example, the exact fourteen-product construction improves the padding-free recursive estimate for LITA \[22\] at _q_=7<sup>3</sup>=343 by a factor of 1.029 (Section 8.1).

## 2 Notation

We will be interested in characterizing the complexity of (multiple) matrix products and tensor contractions. We generally refer to _A_ and _B_ as the input matrices/tensors and to _C_ as the output. Any tensor contraction can be written as a product of (possibly rectangular) matrices by combining modes (dimensions) of the tensors shared between (_A,B_), (_B,C_), and (_A,C_). We associate matrix multiplication with a trilinear form by pairing its output with an independent matrix of variables _Z_:

\(\sum_{i,j=0}^{n-1}(XY)_{ij}Z_{ij}=\sum_{i,j,k=0}^{n-1}X_{ik}Y_{kj}Z_{ij}.\) (5)

This trilinear form is induced by the same tensor as the bilinear map of matrix multiplication. The trilinear form is more convenient for deriving low-rank decompositions of the tensor, which can be used to apply the bilinear map efficiently.

For positive integers _a,b,c_, we write

\(\langle a,b,c\rangle=\sum_{i=0}^{a-1}\sum_{j=0}^{b-1}\sum_{k=0}^{c-1}X_{ij}Y_{jk}Z_{ki}\) (6)

for the trilinear form representing the matrix multiplication tensor corresponding to the product of an \(a\times b\) matrix and a \(b\times c\) matrix. Here _Z_ is indexed in transposed order relative to the entrywise pairing above. We identify a trilinear form with its coefficient tensor in the chosen bases.

A rank-one trilinear form is a product of one linear form in each variable space. For a trilinear form _T_, we write _R(T_) for the least number of rank-one forms whose sum is _T_, and <u>_R_</u>(_T_) for the border rank, the least _r_ for which _T_ is a limit of tensors of rank at most _r_. The direct sum \(T_1\oplus\cdots\oplus T_p\) uses disjoint variable spaces; in particular, \(\langle a,b,c\rangle^{\oplus p}\) denotes _p_ independent matrix products of the same dimensions.

We write multi-indices in bold, for example **i**=(_i_<sub>0</sub>_,...,i_<sub>_d_-1</sub>) for a tensor of order _d_. We use the interval notation \(\unknown 0,d-1\unknown=\mathbb{Z}\cap[0,d-1]\). Throughout the paper, \(F=\unknown 0,d-1\unknown\) denotes the set of positions in a _d_-component multi-index, with _d_ specified for each construction. Thus \(r\in F\) labels a position, while _i<sub>r</sub>_ is its index value. All set complements are relative to this coordinate set: _S<sup>c</sup>=F_\\_S_.

## 3 Motivation: Symmetric Tensor Contractions

Our starting point is a family of fast bilinear algorithms for symmetric tensor contractions \[35\]. These algorithms reduce bilinear rank by forming a fully symmetrized trilinear aggregate over the index space of the contraction and extracting the desired terms from its partial sums. We use the same treatment of lower-order terms to construct trilinear aggregation algorithms for simultaneous matrix multiplication.

Consider a product between a symmetric matrix \(A\in\mathbb{C}^{n\times n}\) and a vector \(b\in\mathbb{C}^n\). The trilinear form corresponding to the matrix vector product _Ab_ is naively a sum of _n_<sup>2</sup> distinct terms, involving \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n+1}{2}\) variables _X<sub>ij</sub>_ with \(j\le i\), i.e.,

\(T_\mathrm{symv}(X,Y,Z)=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\big[X_{ii}Y_iZ_i+\big(\sum_{j=0}^{i-1}X_{ij}Y_iZ_j+\sum_{j=0}^{i-1}X_{ij}Y_jZ_i\big)\big].\) (10)

The symmetric matrix-vector tensor has rank at most \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n+1}{2}\),

\(T_\mathrm{symv}(X,Y,Z)=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\big[(X_{ii}-\sum_{j=0}^{i-1}X_{ij}-\sum_{j=i+1}^{n-1}X_{ji})Y_iZ_i+\sum_{j=0}^{i-1}X_{ij}(Y_i+Y_j)(Z_i+Z_j)\big].\) (11)

The sum over pairs (_i,j_) with _j\<i_ in this low-rank expansion corresponds to a ‘symmetrized’ form of the tensor contraction, i.e., _X<sub>ij</sub>(Y<sub>i</sub>+Y<sub>j</sub>_) is symmetric in (_i,j_), while _X<sub>ij</sub>Y<sub>i</sub>_ is not.

The symmetrization produces unwanted terms, all of which have lower order. More generally, consider a contraction of an order _s+v_ symmetric tensor with a _v+t_ symmetric tensor that is fully symmetrized (i.e., contract _A_ and _B_ to obtain a partially symmetric tensor in the first _s_ and the last _t_ indices, then sum over all permutations of _s+t_ indices into parts of _s_ and _t_ indices to obtain a fully symmetric tensor _C_ of order _s+t_). When _s=t=v_=1, this is _AB+BA_ with symmetric matrices _A_ and _B_. For fixed _s,t,v_, let _w=s+t+v_ and use _d=w_ in the coordinate and complement notation. The corresponding trilinear form is

\(\sum_{(U,V,W)\in B_{s,t,v}}\sum_{\mathbf{i}\in\unknown 0,n-1\unknown^w}X_{\mathbf{i}|_{U^c}}Y_{\mathbf{i}|_{V^c}}Z_{\mathbf{i}|_{W^c}}\) (12)

\(B_{s,t,v}=\{(U,V,W)|U\sqcup V\sqcup W=\unknown 0,w-1\unknown,|U|=t,|V|=s,|W|=v\}.\) (13)

For each set of _w_ distinct index values, symmetry leaves \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{w}{s,t,v}\) distinct monomials, one per tripartition of those values. Including repeated-index tuples gives \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{w}\genfrac(){pt}{2}{w}{s,t,v}+O(n^{w-1})=n^w/(s!t!v!)+O(n^{w-1})\) distinct monomials. We obtain a decomposition of rank at most _nw/w_!+_O(n__w_-1) by first computing the aggregate \(\sum_{\mathbf{i}\in\unknown 0,n-1\unknown^w}\big(\sum_{U\subseteq\unknown 0,w-1\unknown,|U|=t}X_{\mathbf{i}|_{U^c}}\big)\big(\sum_{V\subseteq\unknown 0,w-1\unknown,|V|=s}Y_{\mathbf{i}|_{V^c}}\big)\big(\sum_{W\subseteq\unknown 0,w-1\unknown,|W|=v}Z_{\mathbf{i}|_{W^c}}\big).\) (14) Its summand is invariant under permutations of **i**, so the distinct-index contribution requires only \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{w}\) rank-one terms, one for each increasing tuple \(i_0<\cdots_w_-1) additional terms. _In this case, some index in_ **i** _is omitted in X, Y, and Z, and hence there are at most n__w_-1 _distinct monomial terms, each appearing at least n times._ **Definition 4** (Linearly Reducible Term)**.** \(|(U\cap V)\backslash W|\ge 1\) _(or similar with U,V,W permuted)
In this case, some index in_ **i** _appears only in one type of variable (X, Y, or Z). We may sum that tensor of variables over the corresponding index to obtain a trilinear form with n__w_-1 _terms (again a tensor contraction with one less index)._ Subtracting these lower-order cross terms gives the stated rank bound. Further examples and complete equations for computing the cross terms are given in \[35\]. In the following sections, we review well-known constructions of fast matrix multiplication algorithms, and show that, when written as high-order tensor contractions, they may be similarly understood in terms of replicated and linearly reducible terms. ## 4 Background on Fast Matrix Multiplication ### 4.1 Direct sums of independent matrix-matrix products For bilinear maps with disjoint input and output spaces, the direct sum is the map that evaluates all of them at once. Hence the problem of independent matrix multiplications is a direct sum of matrix multiplication tensors. The elementary upper bounds \(R(T_1\oplus\cdots\oplus T_p)\le\sum_{i=1}^PR(T_i),\underline{R}(T_1\oplus\cdots\oplus T_p)\le\sum_{i=1}^p\underline{R}(T_i)\) (15) come from applying separate algorithms (rank decompositions). Rank additivity was conjectured by Strassen, but has been proven false for general tensors \[33\]. Rank additivity of matrix-multiplication remains an open problem. For instance, \(R(\langle 2,2,2\rangle^{\oplus 2})=14\) already follows from the Alder-Strassen bound \[2\]: the algebra \(\mathbb{C}^{2\times 2}\times\mathbb{C}^{2\times 2}\) has dimension eight and two maximal two-sided ideals, giving the lower bound \(2\cdot 8-2=14\), while two applications of Strassen’s algorithm attain it. See also Rupniewski \[28\] for more general direct-sum results. ### 4.2 Schönhage’s Asymptotic Sum Theorem Schönhage’s asymptotic sum inequality \[30\] is the standard route from a border-rank bound for simultaneous matrix multiplication to a bound on the exponent \(\omega\). Thus trilinear aggregation algorithms for simultaneous matrix multiplication yield bounds on the matrix multiplication exponent. The asymptotic sum inequality gives much stronger bounds on \(\omega\) than using _m_ independent products merely as blocks of one product of dimension _nm_1/3. For exact-rank constructions, the inequality also has a direct algorithmic interpretation described next. Suppose the construction input to the theorem is an exact bilinear construction of rank _r_ that reduces _m_ independent matrix multiplications of dimension _n_ to _r_ scalar products. At the next recursive level, each scalar product becomes a matrix-matrix product of dimension _n_. We may compute these _r_ products by

applying the same construction \(\lceil r/m\rceil\) times, obtaining an exact construction for _m_ independent matrix multiplications of dimension _n_<sup>2</sup> with rank at most \(r\lceil r/m\rceil\). Iterating this recursion gives a concrete sequence of algorithms, with additional recursive levels used as the input dimension increases, and can yield a better effective exponent \(\omega\). Inefficiency from the use of the ceiling may be addressed by first taking a sufficiently high tensor power of the construction. We now state the asymptotic sum theorem in slightly simplified form.

**Theorem 1.** _(Schönhage’s Asymptotic Sum Theorem \[30\]) Let_ \(\mathcal{M}=\oplus_{i=1}^m\langle n,n,n\rangle\) _be a direct sum of m matrix multiplication tensors. If the border rank is bounded by_ \(\underline{R}(\mathcal{M})\le r\)_, then the exponent of matrix multiplication_ \(\omega\) _satisfies_

\(mn^\omega\le r.\)

_Proof._ We provide an algorithmic proof for the simplified case where the direct sum consists of _m_ identical terms \(\langle n,n,n\rangle\) and the rank bound _r_ is divisible by _m_ in Appendix A. For the general proof involving multinomial coefficients and arbitrary dimensions, we refer the reader to \[30\] or the survey by Bläser \[10\].

## 4.3 The Coppersmith-Winograd Tensor

We first recall the tensor constructions of Coppersmith and Winograd \[15\].

**Definition 5** (Little CW tensor)**.** _For_ \(x,y,z\in\mathbb{C}^{n+1}\)_, the little CW tensor is defined by the trilinear form,_<tbc>

\(\phi_\mathrm{CW}(x,y,z)=\sum_{i=1}^n\big(x_iy_iz_0+x_iy_0z_i+x_0y_iz_i\big).\) (16)

<tbc>For \(n\ge 2\), the little CW tensor has border rank exactly _n_+2 \[14, Section 1.2\]. The upper bound, valid for all \(n\ge 1\), is shown by

\(\phi_\mathrm{CW}(x,y,z)=\mathrm{lim}_{\lambda\rightarrow 0}\big[\lambda^{-2}\sum_{i=1}^n(x_0+\lambda x_i)(y_0+\lambda y_i)(z_0+\lambda z_i)\) (17)

\(-\lambda^{-3}(x_0+\lambda^2\sum_{i=1}^nx_i)(y_0+\lambda^2\sum_{j=1}^ny_j)(z_0+\lambda^2\sum_{k=1}^nz_k)\) (18)

\(-(\lambda^{-2}n-\lambda^{-3})x_0y_0z_0\big].\) (19)

For _n_=1, the little CW tensor instead has border rank two.

**Definition 6** (Big CW tensor)**.** _For_ \(x,y,z\in\mathbb{C}^{n+2}\)_, the big CW tensor is defined by the trilinear form,_

\(\phi_\mathrm{BCW}(x,y,z)=\sum_{i=1}^n\big(x_iy_iz_0+x_iy_0z_i+x_0y_iz_i\big)+x_0y_0z_{n+1}+x_0y_{n+1}z_0+x_{n+1}y_0z_0.\) (20)

The big CW tensor has border rank exactly _n_+2: its flattening in any variable space has matrix rank _n_+2, giving the lower bound, and the following degeneration gives the upper bound

\(\phi_\mathrm{BCW}(x,y,z)=\mathrm{lim}_{\lambda\rightarrow 0}\big[\lambda^{-2}\sum_{i=1}^n(x_0+\lambda x_i)(y_0+\lambda y_i)(z_0+\lambda z_i)\) (21)

\(-\lambda^{-3}(x_0+\lambda^2\sum_{i=1}^nx_i)(y_0+\lambda^2\sum_{j=1}^ny_j)(z_0+\lambda^2\sum_{k=1}^nz_k)\) (22)

\(-(1/\sigma_{\lambda,n})(x_0-\sigma_{\lambda,n}x_{n+1})(y_0-\sigma_{\lambda,n}y_{n+1})(z_0-\sigma_{\lambda,n}z_{n+1})\big],\) (23)

\(\sigma_{\lambda,n}=\frac{\lambda^3}{n\lambda-1}.\) (24)

## 5 Simultaneous Tensor Contraction

### 5.1 The Coppersmith-Winograd Tensor as Aggregated Tensor Contractions

In this section, we show that powers of the little CW and big CW tensors have natural interpretations in terms of tensor contractions associated with tripartitions. As a bilinear map, we may interpret the little CW tensor as taking inputs \(a^{(0)}\in\mathbb{C}\), \(a^{(1)}\in\mathbb{C}^n\), \(b^{(0)}\in\mathbb{C}\), \(b^{(1)}\in\mathbb{C}^n\), and computing<tbc>

\(c^{(0)}=(a^{(1)})^Tb^{(1)},c^{(1)}=a^{(0)}b^{(1)}+a^{(1)}b^{(0)}.\) (25)

<tbc>Following notation we used for tripartitions before, we may label the variables in the trilinear forms as _X_={_X_<sup>({})</sup>_,X_<sup>({0})</sup>}, _Y_={_Y_<sup>({})</sup>_,Y_<sup>({0})</sup>}, _Z_={_Z_<sup>({})</sup>_,Z_<sup>({0})</sup>}, and write the CW tensor as

\(\phi_\mathrm{CW}(X,Y,Z)=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\big(X_i^{(\{\})}Y_i^{(\{\})}Z^{(\{0\})}+X_i^{(\{\})}Y^{(\{0\})}Z_i^{(\{\})}+X^{(\{0\})}Y_i^{(\{\})}Z_i^{(\{\})}\big).\) (26)

Here, we label each component of _X_, _Y_, _Z_ by the (possibly empty) subset of indices that is excluded from the variable. The index space is {0}, and hence the only two such subsets are {} and {0}.

Recall our definition of tripartitions _B<sub>s,t,v</sub>_ in (13), and define all tripartitions as

## 5.2 Aggregation of Tensor Contractions

We approach the simultaneous matrix products selected from powers of the little CW tensor in a bottom-up manner, by considering trilinear aggregation of tensor contractions.

We define a trilinear aggregation of tensor contractions by a subset of balanced tripartitions \(\mathcal{S}\subseteq B_{N,N,N}\). We are then interested in a factorization of the trilinear form corresponding to |S| simultaneous matrix- matrix products of matrices of dimension _n<sup>N</sup>_, all viewed as different contractions of order 2_N_ tensors. With _d_=3_N_,

\(\phi_\mathcal{S}(X,Y,Z)=\sum_{(U,V,W)\in\mathcal{S}}\sum_{\mathbf{i}\in\unknown 0,n-1\unknown^d}X_{\mathbf{i}|_{U^c}}^{(U)}Y_{\mathbf{i}|_{V^c}}^{(V)}Z_{\mathbf{i}|_{W^c}}^{(W)}.\) (36)

For \(j\in\{1,2,3\}\), let \(\pi_j(\mathcal{S})\) denote the projection of S onto its _j_th coordinate. We seek to obtain \(\phi_\mathcal{S}\) from the aggregated trilinear form,

\(\sum_{\mathbf{i}\in\unknown 0,n-1\unknown^d}\big(\sum_{U\in\pi_1(\mathcal{S})}X_{\mathbf{i}|_{U^c}}^{(U)}\big(\sum_{V\in\pi_2(\mathcal{S})}Y_{\mathbf{i}|_{V^c}}^{(V)}\big)\big(\sum_{W\in\pi_3(\mathcal{S})}Z_{\mathbf{i}|_{W^c}}^{(W)}\big).\) (37)

A mixed choice (_U<sub>i</sub>,V<sub>j</sub>,W<sub>k</sub>_) selects one factor from each of the three sums in (37). For each coordinate \(r\in F\), its local multiplicity \(\eta_r(i,j,k)\in\{0,1,2,3\}\) is the number of sets among _U<sub>i</sub>,V<sub>j</sub>,W<sub>k</sub>_ that contain _r_. When it occurs in two tensors, summation over that index contracts the corresponding pair of fibers, as in the trilinear form for matrix multiplication. When it occurs in all three tensors, the summation is over their entrywise (Hadamard) product. For a balanced mixed choice, \(\sum_{r\in F}\eta_r(i,j,k)=|U_i|+|V_j|+|W_k|=d\). Thus, in the absence of linearly reducible and replicated coordinates, every \(\eta_r\) is one and the selected sets form a tripartition.

_We use the same matrix Q as a complex-linear map_ \(\mathbb{C}^n\rightarrow\mathbb{C}^{n+1}\)_. Throughout, the tensor contractions are bilinear algebraic contractions, so no complex conjugation is used._

A simple choice for a centering embedding is to choose _Q_ based on a transposed Helmert matrix \[24\],

\(\forall k\in\unknown 0,n\unknown,l\in\unknown 0,n-1\unknown,q_{kl}=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }

The Helmert matrix is computationally convenient because, apart from a subdiagonal part, each column is a scalar multiple of the corresponding column of the transposed prefix sum matrix, and hence it can be applied to a vector with _O(n_) operations.

We can recover tensor contractions after applying the centering embedding. For example, for any matrices \(A,B\in\mathbb{C}^{n\times n}\), embed them as

\(\bar{A}=QAQ^T,\bar{B}=QBQ^T.\) (42)

Then

\(\bar{A}\bar{B}=QABQ^T,\) (43)

so, after computing \(\bar{C}=\bar{A}\bar{B}\), we recover

\(C=Q^T\bar{C}Q.\) (44)

As an example of how the embedding may be useful, recall the symmetric matrix-vector product algorithm _c=Ab_ from Section 3. We may obtain an algorithm with \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n+2}{2}\) products by computing

\(\bar{A}=QAQ^T,\bar{b}=Qb,\) (45)

then

\(\bar{c}_i=\sum_j\bar{A}_{ij}(\bar{b}_i+\bar{b}_j),\) (46)

and finally recovering

\(c=Q^T\bar{c}.\) (47)

Since \(\sum_j\bar{A}_{ij}=0\), the unwanted term \(\bar{b}_i\sum_j\bar{A}_{ij}\) vanishes without an explicit correction. This example illustrates how the embedding automates cross-term elimination. As we also see later for simultaneous tensor contraction, computing the cross-term corrections explicitly can instead give a smaller multiplication count.

To apply centering to higher order tensors, we apply the linear embedding given by _Q_ along each mode of the tensor. The resulting tensor has zero sum along every fiber.

_The input and output modes are indexed by S, in increasing order. In index notation,_

\((\mu^{\otimes|S|}(T))_\mathbf{j}=\sum_{\mathbf{a}\in\unknown 0,n-1\unknown^S}T_\mathbf{a}\prod_{r\in S}Q_{j_ra_r},\mathbf{j}\in\unknown 0,n\unknown^S.\) (50)

## 5.4 Padding and Weighting

We now handle the replicated cross terms by an embedding into C<sup>_n_+2</sup>. Beyond centering, this embedding simply pads the tensor with zeros, which are used in the trilinear form to annihilate the replicated terms via a suitable choice of weighting in the trilinear form.

**Definition 10** (Padding)**.** _Define the padding map_ \(\nu:\mathbb{C}^{n+1}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}^{n+2}\) _by_

\(\nu(x)=\left[\begin{array}{ c }
x \\
0
\end{array}\right].\) (54)

_Thus_ \(\nu\circ\mu\) _is the padded centering embedding._

The padded centering embedding becomes interesting when combined with a weighting.

**Definition 11** (Weight vector)**.** _Define_ \(w\in\mathbb{C}^{n+2}\) _by_

\(w_i=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
1 & \text{\textit{if}}0\le i\le n \\
-(n+1)^{1/3} & \text{\textit{if}}i=n+1
\end{array}\right..\) (55)

The efficacy of the weighting follows from the following claim.

**Claim 1.** _The weight vector w and padded centering embedding_ \(\nu\circ\mu\) _satisfy the following properties. For any_ \(x,y\in\mathbb{C}^n\),

1. _metric preservation:_ \(\sum_iw_i\nu(\mu(x))_i\nu(\mu(y))_i=x^Ty\),<tbc>

_2._ _linear reducibility annihilation:_ \(\sum_iw_i^2\nu(\mu(x))_i=0\),<tbc>

_3._ _replication annihilation:_ \(\sum_iw_i^3=0\).

_Proof._ Since _w<sub>i</sub>_=1 for \(0\le i\le n\) and \(\nu(\mu(x))_{n+1}=0\),

\(\sum_{i=0}^{n+1}w_i\nu(\mu(x))_i\nu(\mu(y))_i=\sum_{i=0}^n(Qx)_i(Qy)_i=x^TQ^TQy=x^Ty.\) (56)

\(\sum_{i=0}^{n+1}w_i^2\nu(\mu(x))_i=\sum_{i=0}^n(Qx)_i=0.\) (57)

\(\sum_{i=0}^{n+1}w_i^3=\sum_{i=0}^n1-(n+1)=0.\) (58)

<tbc>_by_

\(\Omega_{S,F}(T)_\mathbf{i}=T_{\mathbf{i}_{|F\backslash S}}\prod_{r\in S}w_{i_r},\mathbf{i}\in\unknown 0,n+1\unknown^F.\) (59)

\(\sum_{s=1}^m\big\langle C^{(s)},Z^{(s)}\big\rangle=\sum_{s=1}^m\sum_{\mathbf{i}\in\unknown 0,n-1\unknown^d}A_{\mathbf{i}|_{U_s^c}}^{(s)}B_{\mathbf{i}|_{V_s^c}}^{(s)}Z_{\mathbf{i}|_{W_s^c}}^{(s)}.\) (75)

\(\mathbf{k}\in\unknown 0,n+1\unknown^d,\)

## 5.6 Centered corrections and exact rank

For a fixed-shape conflict-free family, the weighted embedding gives an exact algorithm with rank at most (_n_+2)_<sup>d</sup>_. We now use the smaller centered dimension _n_+1 and cancel replicated cross terms by lower-order aggregates.

Let

\(\mathcal{S}=\{\mathcal{S}_1,\dots,\mathcal{S}_m\},\mathcal{S}_t=(U_t,V_t,W_t),U_t\sqcup V_t\sqcup W_t=F,\) (79)

where _t_=1_,...,m_ and the part sizes may depend on _t_.

Assign independent input blocks _X_<sup>(_t_)</sup>_,Y_<sup>(_t_)</sup> and output variables _Z_<sup>(_t_)</sup> to each S_<sub>t</sub>_. In particular, for \(t\neq t'\), _X_<sup>(_t_)</sup> and \(X^{(t^\prime)}\) are distinct blocks even when \(U_t=U_{t^\prime}\), and similarly for _Y_ and _Z_. The resulting target direct sum is

\(\phi_\mathcal{S}(X,Y,Z)=\sum_{t=1}^m\sum_{\mathbf{i}\in\unknown 0,n-1\unknown^F}X_{\mathbf{i}|_{U_t^c}}^{(t)}Y_{\mathbf{i}|_{V_t^c}}^{(t)}Z_{\mathbf{i}|_{W_t^c}}^{(t)}.\) (80)

The summand indexed by _t_ is the matrix multiplication tensor<tbc>

\(\big\langle n^{|V_t|},n^{|W_t|},n^{|U_t|}\big\rangle.\)

<tbc>**Definition 13** (Centered lifting)**.** _Let_ \(P\subseteq S\subseteq F\)_, and let_ \(T\in(\mathbb{C}^n)^{\otimes|F\backslash S|}\) _have modes indexed by F_\\_S. Define_ \(\Gamma_S^P(T)\in(\mathbb{C}^{n+1})^{\otimes|F\backslash P|}\) _by centering T and replicating it along S_\\_P:_

\(\Gamma_S^P(T)_\mathbf{j}=\big(\mu^{\otimes|F\backslash S|}(T)\big)_{\mathbf{j}|_{F\backslash S}},\mathbf{j}\in\unknown 0,n\unknown^{F\backslash P}.\) (81)

_We abbreviate_ \(\Gamma_S^\emptyset\) _by_ \(\Gamma_S\).

To cancel cross terms that share replicated coordinates _P_, we aggregate all lower-order liftings whose input blocks omit these coordinates.

**Definition 14** (Centered aggregate)**.** _For_ \(P\subseteq F\)_, define_

\(\mathcal{A}_\mathcal{S}(P)=\sum_{\mathbf{j}\in\unknown 0,n\unknown^{F\backslash P}}\left(\sum_{1\le t\le mP\subseteq U_t}\Gamma_{U_t}^P(X^{(t)})_\mathbf{j}\right)\left(\sum_{1\le t\le mP\subseteq V_t}\Gamma_{V_t}^P(Y^{(t)})_\mathbf{j}\right)\left(\sum_{1\le t\le mP\subseteq W_t}\Gamma_{W_t}^P(Z^{(t)})_\mathbf{j}\right),\) (82)

_For nonempty P, the correction_ (-1)<sup>|_P_|</sup>(_n_+1)<sup>|_P_|</sup>A<sub>S</sub>(_P_) _is called a_ singleton, pair, triple_, or_ quadruple _correction when_ |_P_|=1,2,3,4_, respectively. The name specifies the number of deleted coordinates._

Its rank satisfies

\(R\big(\mathcal{A}_\mathcal{S}(P)\big)\le(n+1)^{d-|P|}.\) (83)

**Definition 15** (Mixed trilinear form)**.** _For three selected tensor blocks X_<sup>(_i_)</sup>_,Y_<sup>(_j_)</sup>_,Z_<sup>(_k_)</sup>_, whose modes are indexed by_ \(U_i^c,V_j^c,W_k^c\)_, respectively, define_

\(\phi_{ijk}=\sum_{\unknown\in\unknown 0,n\unknown^F}\Gamma_{U_i}(X^{(i)})_\unknown\Gamma_{V_j}(Y^{(j)})_\unknown\Gamma_{W_k}(Z^{(k)})_\unknown.\) (84)

_Its set of replicated coordinates is_ \(\mathcal{R}_{ijk}=U_i\cap V_j\cap W_k\).

Expanding the inner sums in Definition 14 gives

\(\mathcal{A}_\mathcal{S}(P)=(n+1)^{-|P|}\sum_{i,j,kP\subseteq\mathcal{R}_{ijk}}\phi_{ijk},\) (85)

since summing over each coordinate in _P_ contributes a factor _n_+1. For any family Q of nonempty subsets of _F_, define

\(c_\mathcal{Q}(R)=1+\sum_{P\in\mathcal{Q}P\subseteq R}(-1)^{|P|}(R\subseteq F).\) (86)

Then

\(\mathcal{A}_\mathcal{S}(\emptyset)+\sum_{P\in\mathcal{Q}}(-1)^{|P|}(n+1)^{|P|}\mathcal{A}_\mathcal{S}(P)=\sum_{i,j,k}c_\mathcal{Q}(\mathcal{R}_{ijk})\phi_{ijk}.\) (87)

Retain the local multiplicity notation \(\eta_r(i,j,k)\) from Section 5.2. A mixed choice is annihilated by centering whenever \(\eta_r=2\) for some _r_. If it has no coordinate of multiplicity two and \(\mathcal{R}_{ijk}\neq\emptyset\), its replicated coordinates can be removed by inclusion-exclusion.

**Definition 16** (Correction support)**.** _The correction support is_

\(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{S})=\left\{\begin{array}{ c }
P\subseteq F\left|\begin{array}{ c }
P\neq\emptyset,\text{\textit{and there exist}}i,j,k\text{\textit{such that}} \\
P\subseteq\mathcal{R}_{ijk},(i,j,k)\notin\{(t,t,t):1\le t\le m\},\eta_r(i,j,k)\neq 2\text{\textit{for all}}r
\end{array}\right\}.\) (88)

Let

\(\kappa_s=\big|\{P\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{S}):|P|=s\}\big|\) (89)

and define the multiplication budget for the main aggregate \(\mathcal{A}_\mathcal{S}(\emptyset)\) and the corrections A<sub>S</sub>(_P_) indexed by \(P\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{S})\)

\(\rho_\mathcal{S}(n)=(n+1)^d+\sum_{P\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{S})}(n+1)^{d-|P|}=(n+1)^d+\sum_{s=1}^d\kappa_s(n+1)^{d-s}.\) (90)

**Definition 17** (Mixed products after replicated-term cancellation)**.** _The mixed choices not eliminated by centering and the corrections indexed by_ P(S) _are_

\(\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{S})=\{(i,j,k)\notin\{(t,t,t):1\le t\le m\}:\eta_r(i,j,k)\le 1\text{\textit{for every}}r\in F\}.\) (91)

For \((i,j,k)\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{S})\), the remaining term is \(\phi_{ijk}\) of Definition 15. When the three selected part sizes sum to _d_, every local multiplicity in a choice in B(S) equals one and \(\phi_{ijk}\) is itself a matrix multiplication trilinear form. If the selected part sizes sum to less than _d_, coordinates with \(\eta_r=0\) remain and \(\phi_{ijk}\) is a centered trilinear form rather than a matrix multiplication tensor.

For each replicated intersection, inclusion-exclusion subtracts the aggregate with one coordinate deleted, adds those with two coordinates deleted, and continues over its subsets. This preserves the desired products and cancels every mixed product with a replicated coordinate. The following identity gives both the remaining terms and the cost of these corrections.

**Lemma 6** (Centered correction identity)**.** _Define_<tbc>

\(\Phi_\mathcal{S}=\sum_{P\in\{\emptyset\}\cup\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{S})}(-1)^{|P|}(n+1)^{|P|}\mathcal{A}_\mathcal{S}(P).\) (92)

<tbc>_For the target form_ \(\phi_\mathcal{S}\) _defined in_ (80),<tbc>

\(\Phi_\mathcal{S}=\phi_\mathcal{S}+\sum_{(i,j,k)\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{S})}\phi_{ijk},R(\Phi_\mathcal{S})\le\rho_\mathcal{S}(n).\) (93)

<tbc>_Proof._ Apply (87) with Q=P(S). For a diagonal choice, \(\mathcal{R}_{ttt}=\emptyset\) and _Q<sup>T</sup>Q=I<sub>n</sub>_ recovers the desired product. If some \(\eta_r=2\), then \(\phi_{ijk}=0\) by centering. For every remaining choice with \(\mathcal{R}_{ijk}\neq\emptyset\), all its nonempty subsets belong to P(S), so

\(c_{\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{S})}(\mathcal{R}_{ijk})=\sum_{P\subseteq\mathcal{R}_{ijk}}(-1)^{|P|}=0.\) (94)

The other non-diagonal choices are exactly B(S). Summing (83) over the evaluated aggregates gives the rank bound.

For a fixed-shape family \(\mathcal{S}\subseteq B_{s,t,v}\), every mixed choice has

\(\sum_{r\in F}\eta_r(i,j,k)=|U_i|+|V_j|+|W_k|=t+s+v=d.\) (95)

Hence a choice with \(\eta_r\le 1\) for all _r_ must have \(\eta_r=1\) for every _r_. In this case B(S) consists exactly of the non-diagonal compatible combinations of Definition 7.

If this fixed-shape family is conflict-free, no mixed products remain, so the identity is already an exact algorithm.

Splitting the weighted aggregate of Algorithm 1 by the coordinates _P_ at the padded index _n_+1 gives

\(\Phi_\mathcal{S}^\mathrm{wt}=\sum_{P\subseteq F}(-1)^{|P|}(n+1)^{|P|}\mathcal{A}_\mathcal{S}(P).\) (96)

Padding leaves only blocks that omit _P_, and their three weight factors multiply to (-1)<sup>|_P_|</sup>(_n_+1)<sup>|_P_|</sup>. Thus the weighted algorithm evaluates all subsets, while the corrected algorithm retains only those needed.

Since P(S) consists of nonempty subsets of _F_,

\(\rho_\mathcal{S}(n)\le\sum_{P\subseteq F}(n+1)^{d-|P|}=(n+2)^d.\) (97)

Thus the corrected algorithm uses at most the rank budget of the weighted embedding, with lower counts when fewer subsets require correction.

## 6 Border-rank bounds by parameter scaling

We now develop border-rank constructions that eliminate mixed products by scaling the variable blocks by powers of \(\lambda\). This suppresses the unwanted products in B(S) of Definition 17, including conflicts between tripartitions, and can also suppress replicated terms without computing their corrections. Desired products have degree zero, while each unwanted product is either canceled by corrections or has positive degree and tends to zero with \(\lambda\). The resulting limit gives a border-rank bound \[9, 37\].

**Definition 18** (Grading)**.** _A grading of_ S _assigns_ \((a_t,b_t,c_t)\in\mathbb{Q}^3\) _for t_=1_,...,m such that_<tbc>

\(a_t+b_t+c_t=0\) (98)

<tbc>_and_

\(a_i+b_j+c_k>0((i,j,k)\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{S})).\) (99)

_The grading is integral when all exponents are integers._

Rational exponents permit rescaling the smallest positive degree of the remaining mixed products to one in Section 7.1. Replacing \(\lambda\) by a suitable positive integer power gives the same family of tensors with integer exponents.

**Lemma 7.** _If_ S _admits a grading, then each of the maps_ \(t\mapsto U_t\), \(t\mapsto V_t\)_, and_ \(t\mapsto W_t\) _is injective._

_Proof._ If _U<sub>i</sub>=U<sub>j</sub>_ for \(i\neq j\), then both (_i,j,j_) and (_j,i,i_) lie in B(S). Applying (99) to these choices and using _a<sub>t</sub>+b<sub>t</sub>+c<sub>t</sub>_=0 gives _a<sub>i</sub>-a<sub>j</sub>\>_0 and _a<sub>j</sub>-a<sub>i</sub>\>_0, a contradiction. The other two projections are analogous.

Replicated mixed terms of positive degree tend to zero with \(\lambda\). We therefore select corrections only for those of nonpositive degree.

**Definition 19** (Corrections for nonpositive degrees)**.** _For a grading of_ S_, define_

\(\mathcal{Q}_{\le 0}=\bigcup_{a_i+b_j+c_k\le 0}\{P:\emptyset\neq P\subseteq\mathcal{R}_{ijk}\},\) (100)

_where the union is over non-diagonal triples with_ \(\eta_r(i,j,k)\neq 2\) _for every_ \(r\in F\).

Correction sets can be shared, so this choice may also cancel terms of positive degree. A construction is _correction-free_ when its selected correction family is empty.

More generally, let \(\mathcal{Q}\subseteq\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{S})\) be any selected correction family. Using the multiplication budget \(\rho_\mathcal{S}(n)\) from (90), the budget for the main aggregate and the selected corrections is<tbc>

\(\rho_{\mathcal{S},\mathcal{Q}}(n)=(n+1)^d+\sum_{P\in\mathcal{Q}}(n+1)^{d-|P|}\le\rho_\mathcal{S}(n).\) (101)

<tbc>For \(\lambda>0\), substitute \(\lambda^{a_t}X^{(t)}\), \(\lambda^{b_t}Y^{(t)}\), and \(\lambda^{c_t}Z^{(t)}\) for the variable blocks in (82), and denote the resulting aggregate by \(\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{S},\lambda}(P)\). Then<tbc>

\(\Phi_{\mathcal{S},\mathcal{Q}}(\lambda)=\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{S},\lambda}(\emptyset)+\sum_{P\in\mathcal{Q}}(-1)^{|P|}(n+1)^{|P|}\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{S},\lambda}(P).\) (102)

<tbc>Applying (87) to the scaled blocks gives

\(\Phi_{\mathcal{S},\mathcal{Q}}(\lambda)=\phi_\mathcal{S}+\sum_{(i,j,k)\text{non-diagonal}\eta_r(i,j,k)\neq 2\text{for all}r\in F}c_\mathcal{Q}(\mathcal{R}_{ijk})\lambda^{a_i+b_j+c_k}\phi_{ijk}.\) (103)

When Q=P(S), this is the scaled version of (92), with only the mixed products in B(S) remaining.

**Definition 20** (Remaining mixed products)**.** _For a tripartition family_ S _and selected corrections_ \(\mathcal{Q}\subseteq\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{S})\)_, let_

\(\mathcal{J}=\{(i,j,k)\text{\textit{non-diagonal}}:\eta_r(i,j,k)\neq 2\text{\textit{for every}}r\in F,c_\mathcal{Q}(\mathcal{R}_{ijk})\neq 0\}.\) (104)

_When_ Q=P(S)_, we have_ J=B(S) _of Definition 17._

The following theorem shows that this scaling makes the unwanted products tend to zero while using at most \(\rho_{\mathcal{S},\mathcal{Q}}(n)\) rank-one terms for the main aggregate and its corrections.

**Theorem 3** (Border rank by parameter scaling)**.** _Let_ \(\mathcal{Q}\subseteq\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{S})\)_. If a grading of_ S _has a<sub>i</sub>+b<sub>j</sub>+c<sub>k</sub>\>_0 _for every remaining mixed product_ \((i,j,k)\in\mathcal{J}\) _of Definition 20, then_

\(\underline{R}\left(\oplus_{t=1}^m\left\langle n^{|V_t|},n^{|W_t|},n^{|U_t|}\right\rangle\right)\le\rho_{\mathcal{S},\mathcal{Q}}(n)\le\rho_\mathcal{S}(n).\) (105)

_Proof._ By (83), the main aggregate and selected corrections use at most \(\rho_{\mathcal{S},\mathcal{Q}}(n)\) rank-one terms for every \(\lambda>0\). In (103), each desired product has coefficient one, and every remaining mixed product has positive degree. Hence \(\Phi_{\mathcal{S},\mathcal{Q}}(\lambda)\rightarrow\phi_\mathcal{S}\) as \(\lambda\rightarrow 0\), giving the border-rank bound.

The choice \(\mathcal{Q}=\mathcal{Q}_{\le 0}\) satisfies this hypothesis because every replicated term of nonpositive degree has

\(c_{\mathcal{Q}_{\le 0}}(\mathcal{R}_{ijk})=\sum_{P\subseteq\mathcal{R}_{ijk}}(-1)^{|P|}=0.\) (106)

All remaining replicated terms have positive degree, as do the products in B(S) by the grading condition.

## 7 Stability and retained precision

We now study the approximation error introduced by \(\lambda\) and the sensitivity of the bilinear algorithm to round-off error. The first depends on the remaining mixed products. For the second, we distinguish input sensitivity, which depends on the bilinear map, from amplification of errors in the intermediate vectors, which depends on its factorization. The product of the three factor norms bounds the latter. We compare this product with that of classical multiplication and balance approximation error against round-off error at a fixed working precision.

Bini and Lotti analyzed stability of fast matrix multiplication \[8\], and Bini, Lotti, and Romani studied approximate bilinear algorithms \[9\]. Subsequent analyses quantify the effects of recursion, coefficient magnitudes, and scaling \[17, 4, 16\]. We use the product of spectral norms appearing in the bilinear norm estimates of Ju and Solomonik \[21, Theorem 9.1 and Corollary 9.2\] to bound the propagation of intermediate rounding errors. For centered constructions with distinct part labels, the row Gram matrices of the factors are block diagonal, with each diagonal block equal to a multiple of the identity matrix. Their spectral norms therefore follow directly from these scalars, which depend on the tripartition set, corrections, and parameter exponents.

After grouping the modes into matrix indices, write<tbc>

\(X^{(t)}\in\mathbb{C}^{n^{|V_t|}\times n^{|W_t|}},Y^{(t)}\in\mathbb{C}^{n^{|W_t|}\times n^{|U_t|}},x=(\text{vec}X^{(t)})_{t=1}^m,y=(\text{vec}Y^{(t)})_{t=1}^m.\) (107)

<tbc>The target is the bilinear map

\(\mathcal{M}(x,y)=\big(\text{vec}(X^{(t)}Y^{(t)})\big)_{t=1}^m.\) (108)

In the following analysis, vector norms are Euclidean, matrix norms are spectral, and \(\|\mathcal{L}\|=sup_{\|x\|=\|y\|=1}\|\mathcal{L}(x,y)\|\) for a bilinear map L. The norm inequalities below hold over R and C; the centering matrix _Q_ is real with _Q<sup>T</sup>Q=I_ and **1**_<sup>T</sup>Q_=0.

## 7.1 Approximation error

For the selected corrections Q, the remaining mixed products J of Definition 20 contribute to the approximation error with coefficients (86).

For \(\mathcal{J}\neq\emptyset\), let _g\>_0 be the smallest value of _a<sub>i</sub>+b<sub>j</sub>+c<sub>k</sub>_ among \((i,j,k)\in\mathcal{J}\). In the error analysis we divide all block exponents by _g_, keeping the correction family fixed. The resulting tensor at parameter \(\lambda\) is the original tensor in (102) at parameter \(\lambda^{1/g}\). Thus we may normalize the smallest degree among the remaining mixed products to one.

**Definition 21** (Normalized grading and growth exponent)**.** _For_ \(\mathcal{J}\neq\emptyset\)_, a grading is normalized if_

\(min_{(i,j,k)\in\mathcal{J}}(a_i+b_j+c_k)=1.\) (109)

_Its growth exponent is_

\(h=-min_{1\le t\le m}a_t-min_{1\le t\le m}b_t-min_{1\le t\le m}c_t.\) (110)

_For exact constructions, we use zero exponents and h_=0.

**Definition 22** (Parameter-dependent bilinear map)**.** _For a normalized grading from Definition 21, let_<tbc>

\(e_{ijk}=a_i+b_j+c_k((i,j,k)\in\mathcal{J}).\) (111)

<tbc>_For_ \(0<\lambda\le 1\)_, let z stack the variables Z_<sup>(_t_)</sup> _in the output order of_ (108)_. Define_ \(\mathcal{M}_\lambda\) _by_

\(\big\langle\mathcal{M}_\lambda(x,y),z\big\rangle=\phi_\mathcal{S}(X,Y,Z)+\sum_{(i,j,k)\in\mathcal{J}}c_\mathcal{Q}(\mathcal{R}_{ijk})\lambda^{e_{ijk}}\phi_{ijk}.\) (112)

_This is the form in_ (103)_, evaluated with the normalized grading._

**Definition 23** (Approximation bound)**.** _For the construction in Definition 22, define_<tbc>

\(\beta(\lambda)=\sum_{(i,j,k)\in\mathcal{J}}|c_\mathcal{Q}(\mathcal{R}_{ijk})|(n+1)^{|\mathcal{R}_{ijk}|}\lambda^{e_{ijk}},0\le\lambda\le 1.\) (113)

<tbc>**Lemma 8** (Approximation error)**.** _For_ \(\mathcal{M}_\lambda\) _from Definition 22 and_ \(0<\lambda\le 1\),

\(\|\mathcal{M}_\lambda-\mathcal{M}\|\le\beta(\lambda).\) (114)

_Proof._ For \((i,j,k)\in\mathcal{J}\), set \(\bar{X}=\mu^{\otimes|U_i^c|}(X^{(i)})\), \(\bar{Y}=\mu^{\otimes|V_j^c|}(Y^{(j)})\), and \(\bar{Z}=\mu^{\otimes|W_k^c|}(Z^{(k)})\). By (81), \(\Gamma_{U_i}(X^{(i)})\unknown=\bar{X}\unknown_{|U_i^c}\), and similarly for _Y,Z_. Coordinates in R_<sub>ijk</sub>_ contribute _n_+1 each. Group the coordinates retained by all three tensors into **u**, and the coordinates retained by each pair into **a**,**b**,**c**. After ordering the modes accordingly,

\(\phi_{ijk}=(n+1)^{|\mathcal{R}_{ijk}|}\sum_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b},\mathbf{c}}\bar{X}_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b}}\bar{Y}_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{b},\mathbf{c}}\bar{Z}_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{a},\mathbf{c}}.\) (115)

For each matrix slice, use \(|\langle AB,C\rangle|\le\|A\|_F\|B\|_F\|C\|_F\). Bound one slice norm by its full tensor norm and apply Cauchy-Schwarz to the other two slice norms. The isometry of \(\mu\) then gives

\(|\phi_{ijk}|\le(n+1)^{|\mathcal{R}_{ijk}|}\|X^{(i)}\|_F\|Y^{(j)}\|_F\|Z^{(k)}\|_F.\) (116)

For \(0<\lambda\le 1\), apply the triangle inequality to (112) and bound each block norm by the norm of its stacked vector. Taking the supremum over unit vectors gives \(\|\mathcal{M}_\lambda-\mathcal{M}\|\le\beta(\lambda)\).

## 7.2 Round-off analysis of the bilinear algorithms The approximation bound does not account for errors made while evaluating the algorithm in finite precision. We distinguish sensitivity to the input data from the additional errors introduced by the factorization. A bilinear algorithm is represented by a triple of factor matrices \(\Xi=(A,B,C)\) with _r_ columns. Writing their columns as \(a_\ell,b_\ell,c_\ell\), its evaluation is \(z=C\big((A^Tx)\odot(B^Ty)\big)=\sum_{\ell=1}^rc_\ell(a_\ell^Tx)(b_\ell^Ty).\) (117) Here \(\odot\) denotes entrywise multiplication: \((u\odot v)_\ell=u_\ell v_\ell\). **Definition 24** (Spectral-norm product)**.** _For a bilinear algorithm_ \(\Xi=(A,B,C)\)_, define_ \(\sigma(\Xi)=\|A\|_2\|B\|_2\|C\|_2.\) (118) The factorization specifies two linear input maps, the entrywise product, and a linear output map. It does not prescribe how the linear maps are applied. Their implementations may use different summation orders, compensated summation, or factorizations of the coefficient matrices rather than direct matrix–vector multiplication. These choices can affect round-off error \[4, 21\]. We analyze the propagation of errors in the inputs and outputs of these stages. Specifically, we hold _A,B,C_ exact and model each stage as an exact operation followed by rounding its result at the working precision. The errors in the intermediate vectors _ATx_, _BTy_, and their entrywise product depend on the chosen factorization. In contrast, perturbing the original inputs and then evaluating exactly depends only on the bilinear map, and rounding the final result is relative to that result. The next lemma shows how these norms bound errors introduced in the intermediate vectors. It keeps the contribution of the original input perturbations separate, using the norm of the bilinear map rather than replacing it by \(\sigma(\Xi)\). The latter replacement also gives a valid upper bound, as in \[21, Theorem 9.1\], but does not distinguish input sensitivity from errors caused by the algorithm. **Lemma 9** (Input sensitivity and intermediate round-off)**.** _Let_ \(\Xi=(A,B,C)\) _evaluate the bilinear map_ L _in_ (117)_, and let z_=L(_x,y). For_ \(0<\epsilon<1\)_, suppose_ \(\widehat{x}=x+\delta x,\widehat{y}=y+\delta y,\|\delta x\|_2\le\epsilon\|x\|_2,\|\delta y\|_2\le\epsilon\|y\|_2.\) (119) _Let_ fl _satisfy_ \(\|\mathrm{fl}(v)-v\|_2\le\epsilon\|v\|_2\) _for every rounded vector, and compute_ \(\widehat{u}=\mathrm{fl}(A^T\widehat{x}),\widehat{v}=\mathrm{fl}(B^T\widehat{y}),\widehat{w}=\mathrm{fl}(\widehat{u}\odot\widehat{v}),\widehat{z}=\mathrm{fl}(C\widehat{w}).\) (120) _Then_ \(\|\widehat{z}-z\|_2\le\big((1+\epsilon)^3-1\big)\big[\|\mathcal{L}\|+(1+\epsilon)^3\sigma(\Xi)\big]\|x\|_2\|y\|_2.\) (121) _Proof._ First fix the supplied inputs \(\widehat{x},\widehat{y}\). Set \(u=A^T\widehat{x}\), \(v=B^T\widehat{y}\), \(\delta u=\widehat{u}-u\), \(\delta v=\widehat{v}-v\), and \(\delta w=\widehat{w}-\widehat{u}\odot\widehat{v}\). Then \(\widehat{w}-u\odot v=\delta u\odot v+u\odot\delta v+\delta u\odot\delta v+\delta w.\) (122) The rounding bounds give \(\|\delta u\|_2\le\epsilon\|u\|_2\), \(\|\delta v\|_2\le\epsilon\|v\|_2\), and \(\|\delta w\|_2\le\epsilon(1+\epsilon)^2\|u\|_2\|v\|_2\). \(\le\big((1+\epsilon)^3-1\big)\|C\|_2\|A\|_2\|B\|_2\|\widehat{x}\|_2\|\widehat{y}\|_2.\) (123) This is the error introduced by the three intermediate roundings. The original input perturbations instead satisfy, by bilinearity, \(\|\mathcal{L}(\widehat{x},\widehat{y})-\mathcal{L}(x,y)\|_2\le(2\epsilon+\epsilon^2)\|\mathcal{L}\|\|x\|_2\|y\|_2.\) (124) Finally, rounding \(C\widehat{w}\) and adding and subtracting \(\mathcal{L}(\widehat{x},\widehat{y})\) gives \(\|\widehat{z}-z\|_2\le(1+\epsilon)\|C\widehat{w}-\mathcal{L}(\widehat{x},\widehat{y})\|_2\)
\(+(1+\epsilon)\|\mathcal{L}(\widehat{x},\widehat{y})-z\|_2+\epsilon\|z\|_2.\) (125) Use \(\|\widehat{x}\|_2\|\widehat{y}\|_2\le(1+\epsilon)^2\|x\|_2\|y\|_2\) and \(\|z\|_2\le\|\mathcal{L}\|\|x\|_2\|y\|_2\). The coefficient of \(\|\mathcal{L}\|\) is \((1+\epsilon)(2\epsilon+\epsilon^2)+\epsilon=(1+\epsilon)^3-1\), which proves the bound.

To first order, the two contributions to the bound are \(3\epsilon\|\mathcal{L}\|\|x\|_2\|y\|_2\) and \(3\epsilon\sigma(\Xi)\|x\|_2\|y\|_2\), respectively. With exact original inputs and no rounding of the final output, only (123) is needed. The assumptions exclude overflow and underflow and also apply to complex vectors with the stated normwise bounds.

Within this error model, the intermediate-error bound is sharp in general, but need not have the best constant for a particular factorization. ## 7.4 Parameter choice and retained accuracy

Making \(\lambda\) smaller reduces the approximation error but can increase round-off amplification in the intermediate vectors. With smallest remaining degree one, these contributions have orders \(\lambda\) and \(\epsilon\lambda^{-h}\). The contribution independent of the factorization is of order \(\epsilon\). Thus for _h\>_0, the balance determining the limiting loss of precision is between the approximation and intermediate-rounding errors. All limits in this subsection keep the construction, local dimension, and input vectors fixed.

**Definition 26** (Fraction of retained accuracy)**.** _For x,y with_ \(\mathcal{M}(x,y)\neq 0\) _and a parameter choice_ \(\lambda=\lambda(\epsilon)\in(0,1]\)_, define the relative-error bounds_

\(e(\epsilon,x,y)=\frac{\|x\|_2\|y\|_2}{\|\mathcal{M}(x,y)\|_2}\big[(1+\epsilon)^3\beta(\lambda)+\big((1+\epsilon)^3-1\big)\big(1+(1+\epsilon)^3\sigma(\Xi(\lambda))\big)\big],\) (142)

\(e_c(\epsilon,x,y)=\frac{\|x\|_2\|y\|_2}{\|\mathcal{M}(x,y)\|_2}\big((1+\epsilon)^3-1\big)\big(1+(1+\epsilon)^3\sigma_c\big).\) (143)

_For_ \(0<e(\epsilon,x,y),e_c(\epsilon,x,y)<1\)_, the fraction of classical-reference accuracy retained by the bound is_

\(\theta(\epsilon,x,y)=\frac{log(1/e(\epsilon,x,y))}{log(1/e_c(\epsilon,x,y))}.\) (144)

_The limiting fraction is_ \(\theta=lim_{\epsilon\rightarrow 0}\theta(\epsilon,x,y)\)_, when this limit exists._

The two bounds include the same model for input and output rounding. Their algorithm-dependent terms use \(\sigma(\Xi(\lambda))\) and \(\sigma_c\), respectively. The logarithms measure the digits guaranteed by these bounds; their ratio need not equal the limiting fraction at a particular working precision.

## Search algorithm.

We searched for constructions using several algorithms: randomized greedy selection, replacement of tripartitions, search over discretized exponents, and linear and mixed-integer programming. We retain the feasible constructions found by these algorithms. The following describes the joint search over tripartition sets and exponents used for the comparisons.

For balanced families, the candidates are the (3_N_)!/(_N_!)<sup>3</sup> tripartitions in _B<sub>N,N,N</sub>_. A local update removes a random subset of the current family and scans the candidates in random order to refill it. A candidate is accepted only when the three part projections remain injective and a feasible pair of grid exponents (_a<sub>t</sub>,b<sub>t</sub>_) is available, with _c<sub>t</sub>_=-_a<sub>t</sub>-b<sub>t</sub>_. The procedure periodically starts from the empty family and occasionally accepts a lower-scoring family to explore other choices. Stored constructions also supply starting families.

For a nonexact construction and a requested retained fraction \(0<\vartheta<1\), we use \(\mathcal{Q}=\mathcal{Q}_{\le 0}\) from Definition 19 and maximize \(pn^{3N}/\rho_{\mathcal{S},\mathcal{Q}}(n)\). For each candidate, we recompute _c_<sub>Q</sub>(R_<sub>ijk</sub>_) for every mixed product not annihilated by centering. Let _g_ be the smallest remaining degree and _h_<sub>0</sub>=-min_<sub>t</sub>a<sub>t</sub>_-min_<sub>t</sub>b<sub>t</sub>_-min_<sub>t</sub>c<sub>t</sub>_. A candidate with remaining mixed products is eligible when

\(\theta=\frac{g}{g+h_0}\ge\vartheta.\) (153)

Updating an exponent pair changes the required correction sets, each of which is counted only once. With the tripartitions fixed, linear and mixed-integer programming provide further exponent choices. After each such refinement, we recompute \(\mathcal{Q}_{\le 0}\) and check the attained fraction before accepting the candidate.

The weighted search instead maximizes _p_, since one aggregate always costs (_n_+2)<sup>3_N_</sup>. Weighting eliminates all replicated products, so only nonreplicated mixed products constrain its grading. Each tripartition set is evaluated with both embeddings, and each construction remains eligible at all weaker accuracy requirements. For incomplete tripartitions, the code also supports local replacement with objective \(\sum_tn^{\omega|G_t|/3}\) at trial values of \((n,\omega)\), and mixed-integer selection from an explicitly enumerated candidate set.

The normalized height _h_ determines the growth \(\lambda^{-h}\) of \(\sigma\), while the leading approximation coefficient \(\beta'(0)\) of Definition 23 includes only mixed products of smallest positive degree, weighted by |_c_<sub>Q</sub>(R_<sub>ijk</sub>_)|(_n_+1)<sup>|R_<sub>ijk</sub>_|</sup>.  5 gives these quantities and the normalized leading coefficient \(\sigma_0/\sigma_c\) (Definition 25) for the approximate families. Reducing the count at a prescribed limiting fraction does not minimize the error bound at fixed precision: omitting replicated corrections can substantially increase \(\beta'(0)\). The parameter rule balances the first approximation term against the leading intermediate-rounding term. This minimizes their sum when _h_=1, but need not do so for other heights. Neither the limiting retained fraction nor balancing, or even minimizing, these error bounds necessarily selects the most stable or fastest construction at a fixed working precision. The bounds are conservative, and multiplication counts omit encoding, decoding, and data movement. Searches intended for an implementation should therefore account for error constants and higher-order approximation terms, the evaluation order, and measured execution costs at the precision and dimensions of interest.

## A Recursive Proof of the Equal-Size Asymptotic Sum Bound

Assume that an exact rank-_r_ construction computes a direct sum of _m_ independent products \(\langle n,n,n\rangle\), and that _m_ divides _r_. Apply this construction to \(n\times n\) block matrices whose blocks have size \(n^{k-1}\times n^{k-1}\). The construction reduces the _m_ products of block matrices to _r_ independent products of blocks. Partition these _r_ block products into _r/m_ groups of _m_ and compute each group recursively by the same construction. If _R<sub>k</sub>_ denotes the resulting rank for _m_ independent products of dimension _n<sup>k</sup>_, then

\(R_1=r,R_k=\frac{r}{m}R_{k-1},\) (166)

and hence

\(R_k=m\left(\frac{r}{m}\right)^k.\) (167)

In particular, one product of dimension _n<sup>k</sup>_ has rank at most _R<sub>k</sub>_. Taking _k_th roots and passing to the limit gives

\(n^\omega\le\frac{r}{m},\) (168)

or equivalently \(mn^\omega\le r\). If _m_ does not divide _r_, the same limit follows by applying the divisible case to the \(\ell\)th tensor power with rank bound \(m^\ell\lceil(r/m)^\ell\rceil\), taking \(\ell\)th roots, and letting \(\ell\rightarrow\infty\).

### E.2 Norms of the incomplete big-CW restrictions

For the rational degeneration defining \(\phi_\mathrm{BCW}\) in Section 4, distribute the absolute scalar coefficient of each rank-one term equally among its three factors. Put its sign in the output factor. For \(0<\lambda<1/n\), set \(t=1-n\lambda\). Up to column signs, each factor has columns

\(\lambda^{-2/3}(e_0+\lambda e_i)(1\le i\le n),\lambda^{-1}\left(e_0+\lambda^2\sum_{i=1}^ne_i\right),t^{1/3}\lambda^{-1}e_0+\lambda^2t^{-2/3}e_{n+1}.\) (183)

Summing their outer products and restricting to the span of _e_<sub>0</sub>, \(n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^ne_i\), and _e_<sub>_n_+1</sub> gives

\(H(\lambda)=\left(\begin{array}{ c c c }
n\lambda^{-4/3}+\lambda^{-2}(1+t^{2/3}) & \sqrt{n}(\lambda^{-1/3}+1) & \lambda t^{-1/3} \\
\sqrt{n}(\lambda^{-1/3}+1) & \lambda^{2/3}+n\lambda^2 & 0 \\
\lambda t^{-1/3} & 0 & \lambda^4t^{-4/3}
\end{array}\right).\) (184)

The remaining _n_-1 directions in the middle block have eigenvalue \(\lambda^{2/3}\). A retained variable block has a word \(\alpha\in\{0,1,2\}^d\), determined by its scalar, active, and barred coordinates of the variable blocks in Lemma 2. For each variable space, form the matrix indexed by its retained words,

\(G_{\alpha\beta}(\lambda)=\prod_{j=0}^{d-1}H_{\alpha_j\beta_j}(\lambda).\) (185)

The factor’s squared spectral norm is \(\lambda_\mathrm{max}(G)\). Indeed, decomposing each middle coordinate into its sum and orthogonal complement splits the Gram matrix into invariant subspaces. Each other invariant block is entrywise bounded by a principal submatrix of _G_: an orthogonal middle-coordinate direction replaces _H_<sub>11</sub> by \(\lambda^{2/3}\le H_{11}\). All entries are nonnegative, so monotonicity of the spectral radius and the principal-submatrix bound give no larger eigenvalue. The product of the three square roots gives \(\sigma(\Xi(\lambda))\) without forming the tensor-power factors.
